newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Utility regulators aim to become obsolete.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Utility regulators aim to become obsolete.

text.p: Utility regulators aim to reach a point where their industry oversight is no longer needed, officials from North America and Britain told a conference on Wednesday.
"It's very difficult to give up one's job but obviously one has to move towards more deregulation," said Marie Rounding, chair of the Ontario Energy Board of Canada.

"The most important, yet the most difficult, task for energy regulators to deal with over the next five years will be managing the transition from regulation to competition," she told the Strategic Planning Society's conference "Where are the Utilties Going?"
"My mission now is that we will move in most areas to being a competition authority not a regulatory authority," said Clare Spottiswoode, head of Britain's gas industry watchdog Ofgas.
President of the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) P Gregory Conlan said he felt "competition where there is a contestable market" was the solution for regulators.
He said in California only the "narrow monopoly functions" of the natural gas, telecommunications and electricity industries would still be regulated in five years.
"The only reason there would be price caps...would be that the player is too big for the market."
He suggested that a market with a minimum of three players, none of whom controlled more than a percent share, would not need price controls.

But Hector Olea, chairman of Mexico's Energy Regulatory Commission, said he felt competition was only one means of making markets efficient, although he conceded the board's role was to restrict regulation only to monopoly situations.
Rounding said that regulators should endeavour to facilitate competition and thereby minimize the need for regulation.
But there was some disagreement on the best framework for regulators to achieve these aims, with Spottiswoode championing the British system of individual regulators rather than boards.
"I think it's a very good system," she said, allowing relatively fast decisions while regulators could still call on experts for advice, she said.
"I don't happen myself to think the quality of decision making would improve" if there were a board for the regulators.
Conlon said he felt "five (regulatory board members) is a good number," although he later acknowledged the need to obtain a majority vote for decisions was sometimes a difficulty.
Ontario's Rounding, who works with 10 commissioners to oversee all utility regulation, said she felt that as industries converged it would become more important to have a single regulator.
